title: Opportunity for Land Value Tax in New Zealand (Stephen Hoskins, Progress and Poverty Institute, 12 Nov 2026)

content_summary: ELECTION (RNZ snapshot, 8 Nov 2026 3:45am, '100% counted', label 'Preliminary result'): 131 seats including 11 overhang seats (standard 120 + 11); Opportunity 144,298 party votes, 6.0%, 7 seats (0 electorate, 7 list); National 706,680 (29.2%) 42 seats; Labour 710,330 (29.4%) 36; Greens 321,902 (13.3%) 16; ACT 264,121 (10.9%) 13; NZ First 236,630 (9.8%) 12; Te Pati Maori 13,845 (0.6%) 5; total 2,418,565 votes, 131 seats; 66 to govern. Seats sum 42+36+16+13+12+7+5=131. RNZ text: 'Election night results are preliminary, and don't include special votes... Official results are expected on 27 November.' Preliminary results 'become official when declared by the Electoral Commission.' Hoskins's figures agree: about 6%, 7 of 131, 'just shy of 150,000 votes' (actual 144,298), governing bloc National+ACT+NZ First 67 seats vs 66 needed (matches 42+13+12=67). Hoskins does NOT mention the 11 overhang seats; the Commission's own page, the 27 Nov declaration and special votes (which 'usually lean left' per Hoskins) could change seats. Party renamed from 'The Opportunity Party/TOP' to 'Opportunity' in Nov 2025 (Hoskins fn 1). Leader Qiulae Wong. TOP TAX RESET (TOP's own PDF, May 2026): LVT 1.75% on urban and 0.5% on rural unimproved land value (p.5-6, s.2.1); base 'approximately $1.7 trillion nationally', revenue 'approximately $24 billion annually' (p.6; FAQ table: Land Value Tax $24,323m); exemptions: communally-owned Maori land, conservation land (public and private), clubs/societies/non-commercial religious bodies, local and central government land, treaty settlement land, social housing (p.6); deferral for superannuitants until sale, limited deferral for farms (p.7); Citizen's Income $19,400/yr to every citizen/resident aged 18+, equal to the Jobseeker benefit, replacing Jobseeker, Sole Parent Support, Student Allowance, Supported Living (p.4); income tax brackets 28% to $50,000, 34% to $200,000, 39% above (p.4); 'Those earning less than $60,000 per year will pay less income tax than the Citizens' Income they receive'; party projects 10-15% property price fall (FAQ); package 'fiscally positive', ~$4bn net extra Crown revenue (FAQ). All consistent with what places/new-zealand.md already carries (rates, $19,400, 28%, $24bn, exemptions, 10-15%). Hoskins adds the $1.7trn base and the 'about 70% better off / 20% unchanged' claim (party's own). HISTORY CLAIMS vs sources: (1) 1891 graduated land tax = three-quarters of direct-tax revenue by 1895: NEW to the wiki; Hoskins links Te Ara (teara.govt.nz/en/taxes/page-2), which refused (403) so unverified; landvaluetaxguide says only that the national land tax was 'for several years the largest source of government revenue' (Hoskins's cited secondary). Wiki's McCluskey-Grimes-Timmins paragraph says improvements were partially exempted 1891, fully 1892; it does not carry the graduated tax or revenue share. (2) '90% of councils on land-value rating by 1982': NEW; ultimate source is Keall quoted on landvaluetaxguide.com: 'By 1982 hundreds of rating polls had been held, so that in just 86 years 90% of all municipalities had by poll adopted land value rating, which accounted for 80% of local government revenue.' Keall (NZLVRA, wiki already notes him as Andelson chapter author) is a Tier 2 proponent. Does not conflict with the wiki's McCluskey line ('By the Second World War, land value based rating had become the dominant system and this trend continued through to the 1980s') but is a stronger figure from an advocate; Hoskins says 'councils', Keall says 'municipalities'. McCluskey figure carried: 57 of 74 territorial authorities initially on land value. Same site also says the 90% fell to 'about 40%' after 1989. (3) 1988 ended ratepayer polls: NEW to the wiki (it carries only that adoption/abandonment was 'only by a poll of ratepayers'); corroborated by the landvaluetaxguide text ('the government withdrew the traditional right to demand a poll', Rating Powers Act 1988-89), not primary legislation. (4) 'About 29% of councils rate on land value today': the wiki already carries 29% LV, but dated 2019 (Productivity Commission analysis; 71% CV). Hoskins presents it as current ('today') and footnotes only 8 councils by name (Hastings, Kapiti Coast, Napier, Nelson, New Plymouth, South Wairarapa, Tararua, Whangarei); the cited links nearby are landvaluetaxguide, interest.co.nz and an RNZ rates explainer. It is therefore likely the 2019 figure re-used. TENSION to note: Wellington's consultation document (via events/2026-wellington-rating-policies-review.md) says 65% of councils (51 of 78) rate on capital value in 2026 vs 58% ten years ago and 50% twenty years ago, while the wiki's 2019 Productivity Commission figure is 71% CV; so the CV share is not monotonic across the two sources (different denominators/years). The 65% 2026 figure is the more recent official one; Hoskins's '29% today' should not be carried as a 2026 figure. Also Hoskins: 'income tax overtook land tax during WWI', 'only 5% of land value taxable' (landvaluetaxguide: 5% in 1982), 1990 abolition under Labour, all of which are outside the page's current text. Hoskins's cited NZ research (2009 IRD/Treasury, Coleman and Grimes, Gupta, Tax Working Group 2010, IMF, OECD) is by name only.

Unlike the Commission's local-rating focus, The Opportunity Party (TOP), led by Qiulae Wong, is campaigning ahead of New Zealand's November 2026 general election on a national land value tax' (present tense, pre-election) and the sentence 'As of August 2026, TOP was polling strongly enough to be described as a potential general-election "kingmaker," though both major parties (National ... and Labour ...) have ruled out adopting TOP's tax policies in coalition talks.[11]'. Also the party name: RNZ and Hoskins use 'Opportunity' since the Nov 2025 rebrand; the wiki uses 'The Opportunity Party (TOP)'. TENSE CHANGE: YES.

title: Market Power and the Race for AI Infrastructure Dominance (Marc Jarsulic, PERI Working Paper 642, November 2026)
what_was_fetched: READ IN FULL: landing page (HTML, item2-peri-landing.txt) and the PDF https://peri.umass.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/WP642.pdf (link taken from the landing page; dl2/WP642.pdf; text in item2-jarsulic-wp642.txt and page-delimited item2-jarsulic-wp642-paged.txt; Figures 1 and 2 viewed as images). 8 PDF pages: p.1 cover, p.2 abstract (printed p.1), pp.3-8 text and notes (printed pp.2-7); so about 5 pages of argument. Printed page = PDF page minus 1. No access failures on this item. Cited external sources (Compustat, Barkai, Crouzet-Eberly, Bloomberg, Apollo, FT, McKinsey, S&P, Pimco, Goldman, CAP 2019, Avi-Yonah, Krugman) were not fetched.
verdict: ENRICH concepts/data-rents.md (Capturing or Dissolving the Rent: the antitrust / rent-targeting-corporate-taxes bullet) and, secondarily and optionally, research/barkai-declining-shares.md (one corroboration sentence). NOT a new research page: the paper has no tax design (no base, no rate, no mechanism), its evidence is a back-of-the-envelope Q calculation on five firms plus second-hand capex numbers, and the rent-tax step is two sentences with footnotes. Candidate: if the editor wants a home for the 'rent tax as antitrust complement' idea, a short paragraph in concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md could carry it instead; not a standalone page.
claim_grade: B-claim (unrefereed working paper) from a Tier 1 source under the section 4c rubric: Marc Jarsulic, Senior Research Fellow at PERI, UMass Amherst (former CAP chief economist per the brief; the paper itself states only the PERI affiliation, p.2 fn*). He is NOT on sources/audit/people-tiers.json (no match in tier1_confirmed, tier2 or tier3), so Tier 1 is a rubric judgement, not a list entry. The rent-share estimates are D-claim style back-of-envelope (author's calculation). The proposal is an advocacy-flavoured policy suggestion (opinion/C).
content_summary: Q-RATIO EVIDENCE (PDF p.3-4, printed pp.2-3): Q = market value (equity+debt) / replacement value of capital; persistently Q>1 'a strong indication of barriers to entry' (p.3). Rent share of returns = 1 - 1/Q (fn 4, p.4; derivation from Lindenberg and Ross 1981, Journal of Business 54(1); Marglin 1984 pp.291-304). Validation (p.4): Barkai (2020, J. Finance, pp.2421-2463) estimates the rent share of nonfinancial corporate (NFC) value added rose from -5.6% in 1984 to 7.9% in 2014; 'Estimates using NFC Q show rents trending upward from -1 percent in 1984 to 7.9 percent in 2014' (source: Jarsulic, 'The Scale of Nonfinancial rents', PERI, Aug 2025, fn 6, a prior paper not in the wiki); Crouzet and Eberly (2023, J. Finance 78(4), Table II): NFC rent averaged 3.5% of value added 1984-2000 and 6.7% 2001-2017, against 3% and 5.6% using NFC Q. The Barkai figures are consistent with the wiki's 13.5-point rise (7.9 - (-5.6) = 13.5). Firm Q values come from Compustat, with intangible capital per Peters and Taylor (2017, JFE) (fn 8). Fed Flow of Funds and De Loecker-Eeckhout are NOT cited. Opening claim of rising market power rests on Philippon, The Great Reversal (2019) (fn 1) and Zingales (2017, JEP 31(3)) for lobbying (fn 2). RENT SHARE OF NFC PROFITS: the paper gives no single figure for the 'rent share of nonfinancial corporate profits'; it asserts in the policy section (p.8) that its long-term increase 'is an index of the failure of competition policy'. Its quantified shares are rent in NFC value added (above) and, for hyperscalers, rent in after-tax profits. HYPERSCALER RENTS (pp.4-6, Figures 1-2): five firms (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle); Q values 2015-2024 from Compustat; text says values are 'for the most part well above 2.8' but Figure 1 shows Oracle at about 1.8-2.9 and Amazon about 2-3.7, and Meta and Amazon fall to about 1.2 in 2022, so the text overstates the chart. Method (p.5): each firm's rent share is computed from its MINIMUM Q over the whole period ('to be conservative'), applied to after-tax profits; example (p.5): 'For example, 2024 after-tax profits of $322 billion include an estimated $137 billion in rents' (about 42.5%). Figure 2 shows aggregate after-tax profits rising from about $40bn (2015) to $322bn (2024), rent portion from roughly a third to above 40%. CAPEX FIGURES (pp.6-7): '[i]n 2026 their investments are estimated to amount over $700 billion, or to 2 percent of 2025 U.S. GDP' (sources: Vlad Savov, Bloomberg News, 30 Apr 2026, fn 9; Torsten Slok et al., Apollo Global Management, Feb 2026, fn 10); 'Financial analysts forecast that hyperscalers plan to invest $4-5 trillion by 2030, and there is an argument that their investments will be closer to $7 trillion' (fns 11-12: John Foley, FT, 28 Mar 2026 and Goldman Sachs; McKinsey, 28 Apr 2025 'The cost of compute: the $7 trillion race'); financing: $120bn debt issued in 2025 and $175bn forecast for 2026 (fn 13: Apollo Academy 14 Jan 2026; Bloomberg 16 Mar 2026 on Bank of America forecast); 'top 15 issuers of investment grade bonds'; Alphabet planned $85bn equity issue (fn 14, Bloomberg 6 Jun 2026); off-balance-sheet leases/guarantees treated by S&P as debt-like (fn 15, 11 Mar 2026), Pimco estimates undiscounted $882bn (fn 16, 22 May 2026). Also p.8: Goldman estimate that 60% of datacenter power through 2030 needs new capacity; power additions take 5-7 years (fn 17, undated). ARGUMENT THAT RENT-FINANCED INCUMBENCY DEFEATS ANTITRUST (p.3 intro, p.7-8): rents give incumbents a 'continuously replenished source of funding for lobbying, litigation, and acquisition of potential competitors' (p.3, citing Zingales fn 2) and first-mover capex capacity; hyperscaler AI capex helps them 'defend their existing market power, and expand it into other markets'; 'the standard tools of antitrust -- merger review and legal challenges to anticompetitive behavior -- are insufficient to contain large incumbents with market power, flush with rents' (p.3); 'Merger review and court challenges to fairly narrowly defined anticompetitive behavior proved inadequate to the task' (p.8). This is asserted, not tested: no enforcement record or counterfactual is presented. POLICY PROPOSAL (p.8, printed p.7): 'there is an obvious way to complement antitrust and diminish the advantages of incumbent market power: reduce incumbent ability to accumulate rents. Sensibly crafted taxes on rents have long been recognized as a potential antitrust tool.[18] They could be implemented without harm to economic efficiency.[19] ... a tax on rents ought to be added to the competition policy agenda.' NO tax base, NO rate, NO design (not ACE, cash-flow, excess-profits or Q-based) is specified; the paper does not even say whether the Q-based rent estimate would be the base. Fn 18 sources for 'long been recognized': Jarsulic et al., 'Toward a Robust Competition Policy', CAP, 3 Apr 2019 (author's own prior work) and Reuven Avi-Yonah, 'Antitrust and the Corporate Tax, 1908-1928', in Crane and Novak (eds), Antimonopoly and American Democracy, OUP 2023, pp.359-383 (Michigan repository). Fn 19 for 'no efficiency effects': Paul Krugman, 'Monopoly Rents and Corporate Taxation (Wonkish)', NYT, dated in the text as 31 Aug 1971 but the URL is the 2017 NYT blog (archive.nytimes.com/krugman.blogs..., 2017/08/31), so the 1971 date is a typo for 2017.
existing_wiki_coverage: No Jarsulic needles anywhere in the corpus; the digest has no hits for 'Q ratio', 'Tobin' (only crouzet-eberly body text mentions Tobin's Q at line 61), 'hyperscaler', 'datacenter' or 'data centre' as terms. Related pages: research/barkai-declining-shares.md (13.5-point pure-profit rise, $1.2trn in 2014; 'Complementary rather than fully independent evidence' nuance bullet; 'Bears On' list), research/crouzet-eberly-intangibles.md (the efficiency counter; already in the wiki as the steelman, so Jarsulic's use of its Table II numbers adds a cross-check), problems/corporate-profits-increasingly-rents.md (supported_by list incl. philippon-great-reversal, zingales-political-theory-firm, barkai, de-loecker...; challenged_by crouzet-eberly), concepts/data-rents.md (design menu, antitrust bullet), concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md (instrument comparison table with 'Antitrust / DMA / interoperability' row grade 'B for dissolve'), research/korinek-stiglitz-ai-rents.md (AI-rents theory; rent taxes non-distortionary), research/korinek-vipra-ai-concentration.md (compute concentration; line 127 'No rent tax,...'), research/hebous-excess-profit-taxes.md and hebous-mengistu (the actual rent-tax design literature: ACC/ACE, EPT), research/schwerhoff-taxation-economic-rents.md, objections/taxing-quasi-rents-kills-innovation.md (cites Avi-Yonah and Shanan 2024 'Rethinking Taxing Excess Profits'; Avi-Yonah 2023 chapter is a different work and not carried). Not carried: Jarsulic's 2025 PERI paper, the CAP 2019 paper, hyperscaler capex totals, Q-based rent estimation (1 - 1/Q).
anchor_sentences: Anchor A, concepts/data-rents.md, 'Capturing or Dissolving the Rent' (lines 114-118): '- **Antitrust** aimed at the structural sources of the moat, and the **rent-targeting corporate taxes** covered at ([ACE](/wiki/allowance-for-corporate-equity/) / [cash-flow tax](/wiki/cash-flow-tax/)) for the profit that survives.' Add after it (wiki voice, no process narration): that a 2026 PERI working paper argues rent-financed incumbency (the five hyperscalers' estimated $137bn of $322bn after-tax profit in 2024 being rent on a minimum-Q basis, funding a datacentre capex run-rate of over $700bn in 2026) leaves merger review and conduct cases insufficient and that a tax on rents should complement antitrust, without specifying a base or rate; label it a B-claim, unrefereed, instrument unspecified. Also usable as a counterpoint in the 'Honest Limits' sentence 'The rent share of tech profit is genuinely disputed': the Q-based rent estimate is conservative by construction (minimum Q) but is not an independent measure of rent, since Q reflects expected future profits and intangible capital measurement.

Anchor B (optional), research/barkai-declining-shares.md, Nuances and Limits bullet: '- **Complementary rather than fully independent evidence.** Barkai notes his results are "complementary to the independent and contemporaneous work" of Gutiérrez & Philippon (2016)'. A single added sentence: Jarsulic (PERI 2026, p.3-4) reports a Q-ratio-based estimate of NFC rent share of value added reaching 7.9% in 2014, the same endpoint as Barkai's 7.9% (from -5.6% in 1984; Q-based starts at -1%), and Crouzet-Eberly's 3.5%/6.7% vs 3%/5.6% by Q. That is secondary use of Barkai's published numbers, so the page's own Barkai figures are unchanged; the addition is only that the Q-ratio method roughly replicates them. Low priority.
uncertainties: (1) Scanner premises that do not hold: the paper does not give 'the precise policy proposal' (no base, rate or design; two sentences), does not state a rent share of NFC profits as a single number (it uses value-added shares and a hyperscaler rent/profit split), and does not cite the Fed Flow of Funds or De Loecker-Eeckhout. The scanner's phrase 'engaging Barkai' is accurate but thin (one validation paragraph, p.4). The scanner's '8 pp' counts the cover; text is about 5 pages. (2) Not 'rent' in the Georgist sense of a fixed-supply surplus: the Q-based rent includes expected future profits and mismeasured intangibles; the paper itself uses Q as an 'approximation' (p.4); the wiki's standing caution on contested tech rent applies. (3) Text/figure mismatch on Q 'well above 2.8'. (4) Krugman footnote date typo (1971 vs 2017 URL). (5) The Q-based method values rent against the market-value baseline, so the 'conservative' minimum-Q assumption can still capture the effect of a one-off AI-expectation rise in 2025-26 prices only if Q is above prior minima; 2025-26 Q not shown (series ends 2024). (6) Capex figures are Bloomberg/Apollo/FT/Goldman/McKinsey secondary estimates, partly paywalled and unfetched; the $4-5trn and $7trn are analyst forecasts. (7) Author email in the paper is a personal address; not used. (8) Author tier: not in people-tiers.json; Tier 1 by rubric (PERI, UMass) but the 'formerly CAP chief economist' biography is from the brief and is not stated in the paper. (9) The paper's authority for 'long recognised' rests partly on the author's own CAP 2019 piece (self-citation); the independent scholarly anchor is Avi-Yonah 2023 on the 1908-28 corporate tax as an antitrust tool (not read).
